@paulina.muenzing and Gent Berbatovci, the designers behind the new Berlin-based brand @grandexport.world, make “post heritage luxury products” from disused garments – “each piece becomes a conversation between us,” they tell @mad.e.leiner. ⁠
⁠
For their collection Trophies, the pair enlisted photographer @sharnaosborne, who shot the collection in her signature filmic lo-fi – a canny hedge between then and now, a sort of refrain of the label’s time-slipped designs – alongside stylist @emmawyman, art directors @carinafreystefaniebarth and casting director @julialangecasting. “It’s also nice to start with a team who knows exactly what they’re doing from the start,” Münzing reflects, “because we can go together as we grow.”⁠
⁠
Grandexport’s garments are curious yet entirely logical: they barely resemble the materials they began as, though each keeps the charge it was made with. A batch of counterfeit Sergio Tacchini tracksuits, bought from a man whose uncle had been selling them before the Berlin Wall fell, have been picked apart and puzzled into dresses, with a corset inside, a wired-open neckline and the jacket’s ribbed waistband for a hem. Army tent fabric from the GDR, once woven to be strong enough for any terrain, becomes a camouflage mini skirt and top which button together, come apart and recombine with the layers above.⁠

For their new zine, titled Witch, photographer @harleyweir and designer @dilarafindikoglu traveled to Romania to explore and document the power of modern witchcraft and female intuition. ⁠
⁠
“People have historically been afraid of the natural woman,” Weir tells @dominiquesisley over Zoom. “Her affinity with nature, her intuition, the ability to create life, which is a magical, crazy, unexplained thing that can’t really be controlled or understood.” Long-time friends and collaborators, Weir and Fındıkoğlu share a fascination with the power, fears and mythologies that surround the witch. Here their creative worlds converge everywhere from remote rural landscapes and candlelit rooms. ⁠
⁠
“We were trying to redefine the word ‘witch’,” says Weir. “Everyone is afraid of it because it’s associated with something evil, something dangerous. But we wanted to show that these powers are completely natural and that we all carry them within us.” ⁠
⁠
Witch is published by @idea.ltd and is out today. Read more at the link in bio 📲⁠

“Look into my eyes, can’t you see they’re open wide?” sings a dirty-blonde-bobbed Léa Seydoux from behind a piano in the opening scene of Austrian director @mariekreutzer’s new feature, Gentle Monster, which arrives in select UK cinemas today. “Would I lie to you, baby, would I lie to you?” ⁠
⁠
Seydoux plays the French pop-classical musician Lucy Weiss, whose enchanting mezzo-soprano voice is soon interrupted when her partner, Austrian filmmaker Philip (Laurence Rupp), arrives home to their Munich apartment, crumbling to the floor in a panic. The film follows the couple who relocate with their young son to Bavaria, seeking a slower pace of life after Philip suffers from burnout. All seems well as they settle into their new home in the countryside, but before long reality-warping horror unfolds. The story is observed through Lucy’s perspective, through her shock and isolation, her denial. ⁠
⁠
“I like that it’s told this way, not via the perpetrator, or the victim; it’s very much [about] how Lucy reacts, and how she deals with all these contradictory emotions,” Seydoux tells @rose_dodd in a conversation ahead of the London Film Festival. “I was moved to tears when I read [the script] and I fell in love with Lucy. [...] I’ve had traumas in my life, but never something as terrible as this. I don’t know how I would have reacted, honestly, but I had an immense empathy for the character.”⁠

So the story begins: in May 2024, hundreds of sheets of paper were discovered in a Tokyo warehouse, initially mistaken for ordinary paperwork. They were in fact original drawings by @yohjiyamamotoofficial, dating back to his Paris debut in 1981 through to 1999, drawn to communicate his ideas to the pattern cutters who would make them clothes. ⁠
⁠
There are figures that slump over, coats that seem to catch fire, ideas of dresses conjured with a handful of marks. Most have never been seen publicly. Selected by Yamamoto with fashion curator @alexandre.samson.paris, his daughter @limifeu_official and close collaborators, with design support from @petersavillearchival, they make visible a part of his working life long kept private. Now, we glimpse these sketches for the first time, in a book – Yohji Yamamoto Drawings – published by @thamesandhudson. ⁠
⁠
Samson recounts Yamamoto referring to them as “just drawings”. They were not intended as art objects, but as a way to communicate with the patternmakers. Often he found it easier to draw than to speak. The lines are as restless and expressive as the finished garments are composed. Looking at them again, even their maker was taken aback. “What a creative ‘dessin’ I did,” he tells @georgepistachio. “Now, I can’t draw it.”⁠

Dolce & Gabbana Fall/Winter 2007 Ready-to-Wear collection, presented in Milan in early 2007, is widely remembered as one of the duo’s most forward-thinking and visually striking eras.

The entire collection was heavily influenced by a futuristic, space-age aesthetic mixed with Dolce & Gabbana’s signature Italian glamour. Stefano Gabbana and Domenico Dolce took inspiration from metallic textures, armor-like structures, and cybernetic themes.

The F/W 2007 collection made huge waves in pop culture at the time. Most notably, Madonna starred in the corresponding Fall 2007 advertising campaign, which cemented the collection’s “futuristic dominatrix” aesthetic in the fashion history books

In the original 1999 show, model Shalom Harlow stood on a rotating wooden platform while two industrial spray-paint robots spun around her, dynamically painting her white cotton dress in black and neon lime.

Baby Phat’s Spring/Summer 2010 show brought Kimora Lee Simmons’ signature runway extravagance to New York Fashion Week, closing with a special tribute to Michael Jackson.

Presented at the Roseland Ballroom in September 2009, the collection was titled “Moroccan Kiss,” drawing inspiration from 1970s fashion and Moroccan style. Models walked a glitter-covered gold runway in colorful maxi dresses, acid-wash denim, and sequined pieces, with Kimora describing the collection as “modern, sexy, beachy.”

For the finale, four models walked out to Michael Jackson’s “P.Y.T.,” wearing tops that spelled out “Baby Phat” and glittering gloves in tribute to the late singer. Kimora then took her final bow alongside daughters Ming and Aoki Lee Simmons, carrying her newborn son Kenzo, as the audience gave them a standing ovation.

@bazluhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet, which turns 30 this month, was a cultural reset long before the term entered the zeitgeist. Its influence still ripples through popular culture, from Halloween costumes to references in #Euphoria. With its fizzing aesthetic and punk sensibility, Luhrmann’s adaptation brought a fresh energy to Shakespeare’s 16th-century tragedy, introducing it to an entirely new generation.

At the time, however, the film’s outré approach was met with considerable critical derision. In his two-star review, film critic Roger Ebert declared that “this production was a very bad idea”, adding that it would “dismay any lover of Shakespeare”. He was entitled to his opinion, of course, but audiences clearly disagreed. The film debuted at number one at the US box office, proving that Luhrmann’s take on the classic had plenty of appeal beyond the traditional Shakespearean faithful.

Long before personal style became a carefully curated identity, Lou Reed had already mastered the art of looking entirely like himself. His wardrobe was built around a few recurring elements: black leather jackets, tight T-shirts, slim jeans, heavy boots and dark aviator sunglasses. Nothing particularly extravagant at first glance, yet the way he wore these pieces gave them an unmistakable attitude. Reed’s style was never about looking polished; it was about looking unconcerned with whether anyone approved.

His early years with The Velvet Underground placed him at the centre of Andy Warhol’s Factory scene, where art, music, underground cinema and nightlife constantly overlapped. The influence was visible in his appearance: a darker, more stripped-back alternative to the colourful excess of mainstream rock. But Reed’s image was never entirely fixed. In 1973, he dramatically reinvented himself with a short, bleached-blond haircut, black nail polish, tight black clothing and a studded leather jacket. The look became one of the defining visual references of the emerging punk aesthetic. Photographer Mick Rock captured this transformation, particularly around the release of Transformer and Rock ‘n’ Roll Animal.

One lesser-known detail is that Reed was not simply dressing to fit a rock-star stereotype. He openly resisted being reduced to the familiar image of the man in black leather and sunglasses, describing it as restrictive. In a 1982 interview, he explained that he had always wanted to be a writer and had studied with that ambition in mind. Even his more theatrical glam-era wardrobe, including a rhinestone jacket and velvet trousers gifted to him by Angie Bowie, was, according to Reed, simply a more glamorous version of what he already wore. In later years, his wardrobe evolved towards looser leather, dark knitwear, jeans and understated pieces, including clothes by Rick Owens and Issey Miyake. His style remained recognisable not because it followed a formula, but because it never seemed to ask for permission.

In December 1995, just two years before Titanic propelled him into global superstardom, a 21-year-old Leonardo DiCaprio became the subject of one of the most extravagant editorial shoots of the decade. Photographed by the legendary David LaChapelle for the British style bible The Face Magazine, the series captured DiCaprio at the peak of his „90s heartthrob“ era, right around his role in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet.
True to LaChapelle’s signature kitsch, neon-saturated, and Neo-Baroque pop art aesthetic, the photo shoot placed the young actor into a series of surreal, hyper-vibrant backdrops. The most famous and enduring photograph from this session is titled „Leonardo DiCaprio: Unspoiled“, which depicts DiCaprio lying down on a massive, theatrical pile of fruits and vegetables while holding a bunch of bananas. Other eccentric set pieces from the editorial included DiCaprio posing with a life-sized cutout of Marilyn Monroe („Illusion of Levitation“) and modeling edgy, quintessential ‚90s leather fashion.
Reflecting on the iconic session years later, LaChapelle humorously noted in an interview that the superstar might still harbor a little bit of regret over the fruit-heavy staging, jokingly stating, „I think Leo DiCaprio is still pissed off about posing with those bananas.“ Today, these images are widely celebrated as a time capsule of alternative 1990s celebrity culture and fine art portraiture.

Long before social media turned hairstyles into viral trends, Guido Palau was already redefining what hair could look like. Heads: Hair by Guido, published in 2000, brings together more than 70 portraits documenting his work throughout the 1990s. Featuring faces such as Kate Moss and Stella Tennant, the book captures a decade in which hair became an essential part of fashion identity.

Known for rejecting polished, conventional salon styles, Palau embraced raw textures, unconventional cuts and deliberately undone silhouettes. His approach celebrated individuality rather than classical perfection, allowing personality and attitude to take centre stage. Working alongside some of fashion photography’s most influential names, he helped shape the visual language of 90s fashion, from the grunge movement to the era’s defining editorials.

Photographed by David Sims, Steven Klein and Paul Wetherell, the book is more than a collection of hairstyles. It is a visual archive of a moment when beauty standards were being challenged and imperfection became an aesthetic in its own right. More than two decades later, Heads remains a compelling document of Guido Palau’s influence on contemporary fashion and beauty.

Parisian street style in the 1980s was all about individuality, bold silhouettes and breaking with convention. Oversized shoulders, leather jackets, tailored suits, statement accessories and experimental combinations reflected a decade in which fashion became increasingly expressive. Influenced by punk, new wave, rock and hip-hop, young Parisians developed distinct personal styles that blurred the boundaries between streetwear, nightlife and high fashion. Designers such as Jean Paul Gaultier, Thierry Mugler and Claude Montana helped define the era’s dramatic silhouettes, while the streets and clubs became sources of inspiration in their own right.

Le Palace, the legendary Paris nightclub opened by Fabrice Emaer in 1978, became one of the central meeting points for this fashion-forward scene. Artists, designers, musicians and club-goers gathered there in extravagant outfits, where eccentricity and self-expression were part of the dress code.

Serge Gainsbourg was among the figures associated with the club. Known for his relaxed, dishevelled style, cigarette and signature combination of tailored jackets, open shirts and denim, he embodied a more nonchalant kind of Parisian cool. He returned to the stage at Le Palace in 1979 after a fourteen-year absence from live performance, further connecting his image to the city’s nightlife culture.

@nileshchhabria of @finestardiamonds challenges the perception that diamond sourcing is inherently complicated or unclear. The real concern is an opaque supply chain where accountability gets lost between multiple intermediaries.

Today, global luxury brands expect more from their suppliers:

✔ Traceability — Clear visibility into a diamond’s journey.
✔ Responsible sourcing — Documented sourcing practices.
✔ Industry compliance — Relevant audits and standards, including RJC membership and certification where applicable.
✔ Supply-chain accountability — Working with manufacturers who can demonstrate their sourcing credentials.

💡 The retailer takeaway: Don’t evaluate a diamond supplier on product and price alone. Ask about their sourcing practices, traceability and independent audits.

@szilvesztermako has had a big year. He has photographed major celebrities from Elle Fanning to John Galliano to Rihanna, been featured on cover after cover, held a showcase in New York, and developed a distinct visual language that has made audiences declare that fashion editorial is back.

But we live in a time where the attention economy moves faster than artistic processes. Online users and some publications have noted how Makó’s plethora of cover shoots this year—there are no less than a dozen—has rendered outlets like Vogue, Elle, and Wall Street Journal homogenous. 

In the same calendar year as Makó’s meteoric rise to prominence, some who so recently showered Makó’s work with praise and adoration have begun to express boredom with his aesthetic. Across social media platforms, fans, critics, and commentators began to weigh in. 

“Not the fucking sad, dim box again,” one commenter said. “At this point he might as well just be Photoshopping heads onto the same outfits,” said another.

It’s worth noting that Makó reportedly eschews digital processing, AI, and CGI when creating his images. But furthermore, is the concept really the “same” across Makó’s shoots? Or are we confusing the artist’s unique authorship with our own appetite for fresh new content, delivered at faster speeds than any artist can (or should) have to produce? And in this media climate, is it possible for beloved, standout image creators to build longstanding, legacy careers? Or does the audience gobble them up too fast?

The best person to speak on this is the artist himself. We spoke to Makó about his year, the work he has done, and the peaks and valleys of finding mass acclaim in a world full of armchair critics. Swipe through to read what Szilveszter Makó has to say.

Last night in downtown Manhattan, skincare met contemporary art as luxury body care pioneer @necessaire took over Bortolami for a one-night-only exhibition to bring their latest brand campaign to life. Inside the gallery, oversized canvases exploring the human form lined the walls, setting the scene for an interactive installation that reimagined attendees as works of art themselves.

Throughout the night, guests including Chef Sophia Roe, designer and fashion editor Tabitha Simmons, celebrity stylist Erin Walsh, and esthetician and skincare brand founder Sofie Pavitt were among the guests at the buzzing gallery, taking part in the brand’s portrait studio. Each subject was photographed for a full-body shot and a tight crop of their skin, emphasizing texture and silhouette. The result was an exhibition that unfolded in real time—a live translation of the brand’s “For Every Inch, For Every Body” campaign, and a celebration of the individuality of the human form.

It’s a message that carries significant market weight. Since launching in 2018, Nécessaire has been a frontrunner in the luxury body care boom—a category gaining immense momentum, with Euromonitor projecting 7.1% growth to reach $27.8 billion by 2030.

Last night’s activation proved that as competition intensifies, the brands winning the space are those capable of translating consumer data into high-concept culture. By blurring the line between observer and exhibit, Nécessaire bypassed traditional marketing, transforming a commercial campaign into a living piece of participatory performance art.

Yesterday Nicki Minaj, a recent addition to the MAGA party, appeared at a Trump rally in Michigan wearing a two-piece Gucci monogram suit with matching Gucci Horsebit ‘Donna’ pumps. Netizens took note, especially after seeing the brand’s Spring ‘27 show which seemed to feature cartoonish nods to modern American conservative glamour. Looks 11 and 12, for example, reeked of First Lady Melania Trump, who has been seen in Gucci and Gucci-esque looks in recent years. 

Demna Gvasalia, Gucci’s current Creative Director, is famous for his ironic (or post-ironic?) design approach, often showing high-fashion subversions of tackiness, gaudiness, and class. Therefore, his play at sending what appeared to be Melania facsimile’s down Gucci’s runway could be read as typical IYKYK performance art. But what happens when the performance becomes real life?

The release of Kering’s Q3 earnings reports caused a stir in the industry last week after they revealed bleak results for the group’s prestigious design houses. Gucci stood out in particular for an almost 10% slump in sales year-over-year, as well as its reported worst Q3 in the past decade, which includes that of 2020. 

Gucci’s shortcomings are significant because the Italian brand accounts for an outsized swath of Kering’s profits, but also because it was previously prospering under the leadership of its former designer, Alessandro Michele. Michele left the house in ‘22, and was succeeded by Sabato de Sarno. Gvasalia then took the role in ‘25. 

Gucci’s problems appear to extend beyond falling sales and into a darker, much less manageable territory: Politics. Fascism is on the rise, particularly in the US under President Trump. And as US politics continue to divide into increasingly inflamed camps, Gucci appears to be getting pulled into the mess. Few things can topple a brand’s carefully curated image like becoming the statement wardrobe for fascists—not to mention the most aesthetically illiterate political party on the face of the Earth. 

Minaj’s Gucci outfit signals that Demna’s approach to the brand may be going off the rails. But, then again, there has been a Gucci store inside NYC’s Trump Tower for almost 20 years…

It just seems right for @MassimoDutti to return to New York, a city whose style is defined by the sharp suiting of Madison Avenue, high-fashion minimalism, and the art-world intellect of downtown neighborhoods like SoHo. 

The new store at 575 Broadway sits at the center of SoHo’s busiest retail center just off the corner of Broadway and Prince. True to the brand’s ethos, the store design honors the building’s original architectural elements as well as the character of the surrounding neighborhood. Vintage furniture sourced from local galleries peppers the space, nodding to how local artists and gallerists have decorated their studios and loft spaces for decades, especially in the various sitting areas in the men’s and women’s sections which bookend the store. Sounds like a high-service luxury environment? That’s the idea. 

Fabric content is a hot topic right now, with a hyper focus on natural fibers and premium textiles. Combing through Massimo Dutti’s product inside the new store is an opportunity to get touchy feely; It’s easy to linger on buttery Nappa leather jackets, 100% cashmere sweaters, sturdy cotton t-shirts, and selvedge denim jeans. Stand-out pieces include velvetized jeans, fully reversible car coats, and leather kitten wedges with pillowy insoles.

To demonstrate the brand’s downtown street cred, they have curated an exhibition of Patti Smith photos (and other remarkable paraphernalia related to the rockstar’s career) by fashion photographer Steven Sebring. The show is open to the public at 260 Bowery until October 25th and, for punk rock fans and fashion fans alike, is not to be missed. The exhibition carries over to Casa Magazines in the West Village with a special window display and a city guide curated by Apartamento in their café space. 

NYC is famously tough toward transplants, tourists, and out-of-towners in general. But with Casa Magazines, Patti Smith, and a SoHo space, Massimo Dutti is up for the challenge.

Many countries are working to limit the fossil fuel industry, by curbing advertisements on airlines and cars. These are great efforts to protect people, the planet, and animals 💚⁠
⁠
An issue? These bans largely leave out or fail to acknowledge how fast fashion is an extension of the fossil fuel industries—and how fast fashion and much of the larger fashion industry is contributing to many issues the world faces 😩 From overproduction creating needless waste to harmful synthetics being a dominant materials, there is a disconnect between the industries that “cause harm” and the industries that cause less (or no) harm. Fashion it seems falls into the latter category.⁠
⁠
But, with two splashy (if imperfect) efforts to hold fashion accountable, we may be experiencing the start of a change that could pick-up speed in similar ways to the banning of social media in relationship to teens, which started in Australia and has rippled across the world. At least that is our hope, considering fast fashion has kicked global consumption to unfathomable heights, all while proving stats that the sector affects a third of global agriculture and contributes to textile waste reaching 26.6 million tonnes 🫤⁠
⁠
We must take the issue tied to fashion more seriously as its associated problems are more than “just clothes”. When brands work more transparently while taking on more sustainable practices, fashion can function well. For now, we need change—fast. What are your thoughts on fast fashion ad bans? Heels for the photographs. Sneakers for the party. Sakshi Sindwani (@sakshisindwani) has her hosting wardrobe figured out.

“Start with heels for the photographs, then change into sneakers. Most of my parties have ended with me either barefoot or in sneakers. Once the photographs are done, I want to be comfortable on my feet,” she shares.

Where Is Street Style Headed? A Love Letter to Bill Cunningham

Outside the Dior show in Paris, I found myself asking: where is street style headed? 🤍

I got my fashion wings in the era when Bill Cunningham rode through Manhattan on his bicycle, camera round his neck, in that bright blue French worker’s jacket. For decades, his “On the Street” column in The New York Times documented how real people dressed. Not celebrities. Not runways. Real life.

He was fashion’s cultural anthropologist. He famously said: “Fashion is the armour to survive the reality of everyday life.”

So I’m asking you: has fashion week lost its edge? Is street style now just a sea of gifted head-to-toe looks? 

And who is the cultural anthropologist of today? 👇

Someone once told me I’m not a fashion influencer. I agree. I’m a fashion observer and critic, who quietly puts looks together for herself, loves pink, and loves luxury. 💗

I’m never in head-to-toe anything. Always something borrowed, something new, and a designer to watch. And I love a pre-loved moment. ♻️

A young man draws water from a well. Another tends to buffaloes. A third chops wood in a field. Cut to the same faces, transformed by fashion’s formidable machinery of styling and spectacle, striding down fashion runways. The transitions are cheeky, the message seemingly simple: look how far we’ve come.
But something more interesting is unfolding in the viral hometown-to-runway Reels trend, set to Suraj Tratak’s 𝑷𝒂𝒉𝒂𝒅𝒊 fusion number ‘Swami Pardesh’, that has taken over Instagram in India. For these models, it’s not just about making it to fashion’s coveted catwalks. It’s a two-way flex—showing off their glamorous high-fashion lives while being equally assertive of their reality and roots.
Among those embracing the trend are Chennai-born Savio Fedrick, Rituraj Singh Nabiyal, an IIT Kanpur student from Nabi in Uttarakhand, and Sikkim-boy Dawa La. Structurally, the videos resemble the before-and-after makeover trope. Except the before hasn’t disappeared. Kolhapur model Sakshi Kumbhar transitions from working in a sugarcane field to walking the ramp for Amit Aggarwal. The smalltown girl or village boy hasn’t been replaced by the runway model. Both identities coexist. 
Therein lies a contemporary idea of aspiration: success no longer demands that you repudiate where you came from. For generations, fashion’s rarefied circles demanded sophistication—polished accents, altered appearances and cosmopolitan identities. Yesteryear supermodel Madhu Sapre, mocked for her Maharashtrian accent, reportedly taught herself fluent English. 
In contrast, these models are putting the farms, families, buffaloes and village homes into the frame. Backgrounds once concealed in pursuit of glamour are claimed as badges of individuality. This reflects a larger cultural shift from concealing provenance to celebrating it, even if there is irony in packaging rural ordinariness as algorithm-friendly content. 
Perhaps, the most refreshing aspect of this trend is that its protagonists aren’t debating which version of them is real. The ultimate flex isn’t simply that they’ve arrived on the world’s runways. It’s that they no longer feel compelled to leave home behind.

“The discussion about craft in India is about revival. We’re still looking at supporting craft communities. It’s a narrow way of looking at craft. 
I am a trained textile designer, and work with leftover remnants of fabric. Patchwork developed independently across textile cultures, flourishing at different periods because communities stumbled upon it as a great way to join little bits of cloth together. Kantha and Kavandi quilts are from India. In Korea, Jogakbo were cloths used to wrap gifts; in northern Japan, patchwork reinforced clothing against the cold. In some communities it is celebrated; in others, it is a survival instinct. In a contemporary art setting, where I sometimes position my work, as in exhibitions like 𝑴𝒂𝒔𝒕𝒆𝒓𝒔 𝒊𝒏 𝑴𝒂𝒌𝒊𝒏𝒈, a single artefact can teach a viewer a lot about a craft: Was it woven, dyed, patchworked? It can expand the craft’s relevance by making it speak to the present. 
On the one hand, the term craft is ubiquitous. On the other, people only associate it with a narrative of endangerment. I think expanding our narrative of craft is more crucial than interpreting it narrowly.”

The name of this column was not mine.
Jaspreet Chandok (JC), co-founder and head of business of The Voice of Fashion (TVOF) suggested 𝑶𝒏𝒆 𝑷𝒆𝒈 𝒘𝒊𝒕𝒉 𝑺𝒉𝒆𝒇𝒂𝒍𝒆𝒆. He also named “Questions No One Asks”, an interview series which acquired symbolic value for this platform.
I begin here for my goodbye note because I believe that authorship is more complicated than what a byline suggests.
Today is my last day at TVOF as its editor-in-chief for nine years.
In April 2017, I walked into the IMG-Reliance office at Nariman Point with a proposal for a digital magazine on fashion, culture and design. The coffee was terrible. The questions from those who interviewed me (all named in my full piece!) were tough. Cricket jerseys hung around the room. I got the job I had dared to dream about. A year after that, TVOF went live: India’s first fully digital magazine of its kind, built on a model that did not depend on advertising.
What followed was ‘fashion-fashion’, and then much more. Textiles and identity, the politics of the body, ground reports, sustainability before it became a reporting genre, columns by writers who were not fashion journalists. Retaining the tension between the industry’s contributions and its contradictions without being dazzled by either.
But this last peg is about a harder question. What does it take to shape a voice when your magazine belongs to a corporate group that invests in the industry it critiques? When the person protecting the business of your editorial freedom also heads the fashion week that comes up for reviews? 
I brought in the conviction and editorial judgement, but that alone does not do it. Nor does a declaration of freedom. I have written about what does: the people who held the line, and the uncomfortable truth, that the freedom to question power may itself be partly enabled by power. That’s why I started with JC.
Now about why I am leaving. Because the impulse that helped me envision TVOF has not yet run its course. I want to start building again; a bigger inquiry into India; which includes fashion but goes beyond it. With writing and reporting, of course. But not only.

@raw_mango's woven motifs are conceived through innovation and tireless research, each reflecting an ongoing dialogue with traditional design vocabulary, experimentation in form and technique. 

Come visit us this weekend in the DMV area - at the Sheraton Reston, VA from 11-7pm on Saturday and Sunday. 

Floral motifs are central to their woven lexicon, spanning a wide range - native Indian varieties, those depicted in miniature paintings and ancient sculptures, or tied into ritual.

Often, floral motifs of gulab (rose), kamal (lotus), poppy, cherry blossom, rajnigandha (tuberose), champa (frangipani), mogra (jasmine), pansy - are realised through weaving with extra weft insertion and zari, vibrant prints on silk and hand embroideries. At once evocative and inventive, they document archival designs while also reimagining possibilities within traditional craft.

In 2014, some brick kiln workers in Punjab seeking identity documents and social security registration faced an unexpected obstacle. Years of heat, friction and manual labour had made their fingerprints difficult for biometric scanners to capture. Some were advised to wear gloves and apply medicine before trying again. 

In Pakistan, a failed fingerprint scan can block access to a bank account, SIM card, welfare payment or property transfer. For workers whose hands build, clean and sustain much of the country, the consequences reach far beyond the scanner. 

In the latest Brown History Newsletter, Sunya Sheikh traces fingerprinting’s South Asian history and draws on fieldwork in Punjab to ask what happens when the marks of earning a living make it harder to prove who you are.

On 27 October 1971, Ahmed Timol, a 29 year old South African anti-apartheid activist of Indian descent, fell to his death from the tenth floor of Johannesburg's police headquarters. He had been in police custody for five days. Police claimed he had committed suicide. But his family and many didn't believe them; Apartheid security police were notorious for torturing and killing political detainees.

Timol was a teacher who challenged apartheid inside and outside the classroom. He questioned the government's version of history, using lessons about the French Revolution and resistance to Nazism to help students understand injustice.

Timol was among the school's most popular teachers. He greeted students warmly, treated them equally regardless of background, and disliked failing them, mindful of their parents' sacrifices.

After receiving political training in Moscow, Timol returned to South Africa in 1970 to help rebuild underground networks linked to the banned ANC and South African Communist Party. He distributed political literature while continuing to teach.

On 22 October 1971, police arrested Timol and fellow activist Salim Essop after finding banned literature in their car. Timol was taken to John Vorster Square, where security police interrogated and tortured him. Five days later, he was dead.

His death sparked outrage across South Africa. Thousands mourned, religious and community leaders demanded an investigation, and communities organised prayer gatherings and protest.

However, a 1972 inquest upheld the apartheid police's account: the Soviet-trained activist had supposedly killed himself to avoid confessing to offences against the state. Despite evidence of injuries, the authorities were cleared of responsibility.

His family, fellow activists and supporters continued demanding the truth. In 2017, a reopened inquest finally ruled that Timol had been tortured and murdered by security police.
46 years later, the official story collapsed. Timol never saw apartheid end, but his death became a symbol of the brutality used to silence those who resisted it.

At 3am on 23 October 1971, South African security police raided the home of Amina Desai, a 52 year old widow and mother of four. Her alleged offence? Helping an anti-apartheid activist who used her home and car.

Born in South Africa in 1919, Amina was the daughter of an Indian father and a Malay mother. At ten, she was pulled out of school to care for her younger siblings. Determined to continue her education, she eventually attended a whites-only college in Johannesburg, becoming its only non-white student.

Her husband, Suleiman Desai, died in 1969. Amina took over his business, challenging expectations of what a widowed woman could do.

Her home also became a refuge for Ahmed Timol, a young teacher and underground anti-apartheid activist (second photo). He used her car, typewriter and garage for political activities. When police arrested him in October 1971 and discovered banned literature in her car, they came for Amina.

She was taken to Johannesburg's notorious John Vorster Square police station. During her interrogation, she heard screams and furniture crashing in a nearby room. She later learned that Timol had died in police custody after falling from a tenth-floor window. Police claimed he had jumped. His death became a symbol of the brutality of apartheid and the violence used to silence those who resisted it.

Amina spent months in solitary confinement before receiving a five year prison sentence under the Terrorism Act in 1972. She was imprisoned alongside prominent activists Dorothy Nyembe and, briefly, Winnie Mandela.

Released in 1978, she became South Africa's longest serving Indian woman political prisoner at the time, however, her punishment continued through another 5 years of banning restrictions and house arrest.

In 1996, she testified before South Africa's Truth and Reconciliation Commission. She died in Dublin in 2009, aged 89. Four years later, South Africa posthumously awarded her the Order of Luthuli in Silver.

Amina's daughter, Dr Zureena Desai, also made headlines in 1969 when she and her white partner were arrested under apartheid's Immorality Act, which criminalised interracial relationships (we talked about this two posts ago).

Dr Zureena Desai is a South African doctor of Indian descent whose relationship with a white academic became a major apartheid-era court case. In 1969, police arrested her and her partner, Dr John Blacking, under the Immorality Act, which criminalised sexual relationships across the white/non-white racial divide. 

In Apartheid South Africa, police hunted down interracial couples suspected of having a relationship. Homes were raided, doors were smashed down. Any interracial couple caught in bed were arrested and if found guilty, were sent to prison. Of course, the person of color in the relationship was given a much harsher sentence.
⁣
Police spent hours spying on Blacking’s home. They hid between trees while peering inside his windows, listening through air vents, and even climbed up a tree across the street to see into the bedroom. 

Eventually, the police raided his home in the middle of the night and arrested the couple. Ironically, they put the two in the same cell. Outside, friends and family supported them, alongside people who sent messages from around the world. 

The couple were convicted of conspiring to have sex and received suspended sentences. Their trial drew international attention and exposed the state’s invasive policing of private life.

After the trial, Zureena and Blacking moved to Northern Ireland, eventually married and had four daughters. She specialised in haematology and worked at Queen’s University Belfast and the Royal Victoria Hospital. Blacking died in 1990.

Aparthied in South Africa eventually ended in 1994 (for context, 1994 was the year The Lion King and Forrest Gump was released).
